Reproducibility is limited by reliance on closed proprietary models, default high-temperature settings without repeated trials, and a missing or unspecified code/data URL in the manuscript despite claiming availability.

The paper includes useful controls, especially unmodified-image sanity checks, Y/N counterfactual identification, in-image text injection, background removal, and a linear-probing experiment that points toward a vision-language integration issue.
The qualitative examples are clear and memorable, making the failure mode easy to understand and likely useful to the VLM evaluation community.
weaknesses: The causal claim that failures are primarily due to language-prior bias is somewhat overextended. Many results are also consistent with visual attention, small-object perception, occlusion, image generation artifacts, or general counting limitations; the linear probe supports the claim only for one encoder/domain setting.
The unmodified-image sanity check does not fully establish that models visually count the relevant elements, since canonical images can be answered from prior knowledge alone.

Dataset construction relies partly on generated and manually filtered counterfactual images, but the paper gives limited detail on annotation protocols, rejection rates, inter-annotator agreement, and whether examples were selected in a way that could inflate the observed effect.

Human validation is helpful but narrow, focusing on animal leg counting; broader human studies across logos, flags, boards, illusions, and grids would better establish that all benchmark items are visually unambiguous.

The appendix contains substantial implementation detail for task construction, prompts, model settings, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that failures are due to language or knowledge bias is not fully established. Many tasks also confound bias with known VLM weaknesses in small-object perception, visual counting, synthetic-image artifacts, and grid/stripe parsing.

The definition of bias rate as matching a pre-defined canonical answer is suggestive but not sufficient evidence of bias; canonical-count errors could arise from visual difficulty or generic counting shortcuts without proving memorized knowledge override.

Dataset validity is under-supported. Generated counterfactual images are manually filtered, but the paper gives little detail on annotator count, agreement, rejection rates, ambiguity criteria, or quality statistics across domains. The human study validates only the animal subset.

Several controls are informative but not decisive: background removal changes salience and distribution; the linear probe uses only one encoder and one task; reasoning-token analyses are correlational; API-vs-ChatGPT tool comparisons are heavily confounded.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing work on VLM hallucination, counter-commonsense images, visual priors, and counting failures. The paper’s positioning would be stronger if it more carefully separated its benchmark contribution from broader claims that VLMs are generally biased.

Reproducibility is a concern: the abstract says code and data are available but provides no URL, and many results rely on closed/proprietary models and generated images whose exact regeneration may be difficult.

The writing repeatedly overstates conclusions, e.g. that vision encoders sufficiently encode the needed information or that more knowledge leads to more bias, based on limited evidence. A more cautious framing would make the contribution more credible.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and intuitive failure mode: VLMs often default to canonical knowledge when asked neutral counting or identification questions about counterfactual familiar objects. The examples are compelling and easy to understand.

The benchmark spans several visually distinct domains, including animals, logos, flags, chess/game boards, optical illusions, and synthetic patterned grids, which makes the phenomenon broader than a single anecdotal task.

The evaluation covers many strong closed and open models, plus useful diagnostic variants such as background removal, in-image text, repeated runs, prompting interventions, tool use, pointing VLMs, resolution analysis, and a human baseline for animal images.
The paper is generally readable and the main tables communicate the empirical pattern clearly: accuracy is low and many wrong answers are aligned with canonical counts.
weaknesses: The central causal attribution to language-prior bias is overstated. Many failures could also be explained by generic counting weakness, small or low-salience visual details, image-generation artifacts, model preprocessing limits, or ambiguity in object identity. The paper often treats bias-aligned errors as proof of bias rather than as evidence consistent with bias.

The benchmark needs stronger validation. Manual filtering is described, but there is little detail on annotator agreement or systematic quality checks, and the human study only covers animal leg counting, not the other six domains where artifacts and ambiguity may be more severe.

Several tasks are conceptually ambiguous. Modified Adidas/Nike/Audi logos may or may not still count as those logos; modified national flags may still be recognizable as country flags; optical illusion questions conflate physical ground truth with perceived illusion responses. These ambiguities weaken the interpretation of Q3 and bias rates.

The sanity check on unmodified images is not sufficient evidence that models visually perceive the relevant elements. A model can answer canonical counts correctly from recognition alone, so 100% accuracy on originals does not establish that failures on counterfactuals are caused by overridden visual evidence.

Important controls are missing or underdeveloped: matched unfamiliar/non-branded versions, close-up crops with equal object size, non-counterfactual counting controls, explicit forced zoom/tool-use conditions, and comparisons to specialized counting/segmentation pipelines under the same input constraints.

Some diagnostic claims are too strong. The background-removal result changes salience and image distribution, not just background bias. The linear-probe result is limited to one encoder and one generated animal task, so it does not establish that evaluated VLMs generally encode the needed evidence and are overridden by the LLM. The reasoning-token analysis is correlational and likely confounded by instance difficulty.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on closed-source APIs, ChatGPT/Puppeteer tooling, generated images from proprietary systems, temperature 1.0 settings, and an apparently missing or incomplete code/data URL in the abstract.

Overall, the paper has a promising benchmark and interesting empirical signal, but the evidence does not fully support the strength of the causal claims. I would lean marginal reject for a top-tier venue unless the authors substantially tighten validation, controls, and claim framing.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely failure mode: VLMs defaulting to canonical knowledge when visual evidence is counterfactual. The use of neutral counting/identification prompts is a useful contrast to benchmarks that prime models through biased text.

The empirical scope is substantial: seven task families, multiple strong closed models, newer and open-source models in the appendix, repeated-run checks, prompting variants, in-image text, resolution analysis, background-removal experiments, pointing-model comparisons, and a small human study.

The headline results are striking and mostly consistent across models: very low counterfactual counting accuracy, high bias-aligned response rates, and improved performance after isolating targets from their usual background.
The benchmark construction is reasonably systematic, and the paper provides many task-generation details and qualitative examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central attribution is overclaimed. Many experiments show counterfactual counting failures, but they do not cleanly separate memorized language priors from small-object visibility, image-editing artifacts, occlusion, cropping/scale effects, ordinary counting difficulty, or semantic ambiguity in modified logos and objects.

The unmodified-image sanity check is weak evidence: canonical images have canonical answers, so 100% accuracy may reflect memorized facts rather than actual visual counting. This does not establish that later failures are caused by language bias.

Dataset validity is under-documented. Human quality control is mentioned, but there is no clear annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, audit statistics, or broad human validation across all seven domains. The human study covers only animal legs, not the harder logo, flag, board, and illusion tasks.

Several qualitative examples are too small or visually ambiguous in the paper to let readers verify ground truth. This is especially concerning for car logos, shoe logos, and fine-grained flag/board modifications.

The background-removal result is confounded: removing background also changes crop, object scale, clutter, and rendering simplicity. It supports that context matters, but not the stronger causal claim that background visual cues trigger bias.

The linear-probe experiment is too narrow to support the broad claim that vision encoders encode the needed information while language models override it. It uses one encoder/model family and one animal subtask, and may exploit generation artifacts.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code and data are available but no URL appears in the manuscript/PDF links, and the evaluation depends heavily on generated images and manual filtering.

The statistical treatment is limited. Multiple resolutions and prompt variants appear dependent, task means can obscure unequal sample sizes, and confidence intervals/significance tests are largely absent.

The framing repeatedly uses broad terms like “VLMs are biased” where “biased toward canonical/counting priors under these counterfactual constructions” would be more precise. The writing also has noticeable typos, formatting issues, and occasional overly strong conclusions.
